issues.explanation: Carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile and trauma type. For a 61-year-old married male paramedic whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, the other selected items center on sensory triggers, intrusive recall, and emotion-focused coping. Weapon carrying implies a persistent interpersonal/assault threat context that is not represented in the triggers, memory, or formulation, making this item clinically incoherent here.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is weakly supported by the rest of the selected profile. The formulation shows Threat and Negative Appraisals as inactive, yet shame is a strong self-appraisal-based memory response. With no negative appraisal items and no threat-linked content, this item does not fit the otherwise trigger-memory-avoidance pattern as well as the other memory items.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: For a toxic chemical exposure trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to reconcile unless the exposure clearly occurred in an air-evacuation or aircraft-related context; nothing else in the profile supports that context, so this trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

Dark spaces are not impossible, but with toxic chemical exposure they are weakly supported here because no memory, threat, or appraisal content links the trauma to darkness or confined/obscured environments. In this profile the trigger set starts to imply a different trauma context than the rest of the items.

vignette:
Harjit Sandhu is a 61-year-old South Asian man who has worked as a paramedic for nearly three decades. He is married and has spent most of his adult life running toward emergencies that others flee. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after a chemical exposure incident that he describes as unlike anything in his long career.

The incident occurred on a night shift. Harjit and his partner were dispatched to an industrial facility where a worker had collapsed. The scene was poorly lit, and Harjit entered a storage area in near darkness before any hazmat protocols had been established. Within seconds of entering, he registered an acrid, chemical smell - sharp and unfamiliar - and almost simultaneously began to feel his eyes burning, his chest tightening, and his legs weakening. He recalls the disorientation of not knowing what he was breathing, of calling out to his partner and hearing his own voice sound strange, of dropping to one knee on the concrete floor and being uncertain whether he would be able to stand again. He was evacuated by colleagues and treated on site, then transported to the emergency department. Physically, he recovered within days. What did not recover was his sense of the world as a place where his training and experience were sufficient protection.

In the weeks that followed, Harjit found that the memory of those minutes in the dark did not behave like other difficult memories from his career. It did not stay where he put it. A colleague opening a bottle of rubbing alcohol in the ambulance bay - the sharp, solvent edge of the smell - could return him instantly and completely to that storage room floor, the burning in his eyes, the terror of not knowing whether he was dying. The transition was not gradual; it was total and without warning. When the memory arrived in this way, Harjit described feeling so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to physically stop what he was doing and grip something solid until it passed. Attempting to recall the event deliberately produced the same terror he had experienced in the moment - not a muted echo but the original fear, as immediate as the night itself.

Harjit had come to believe, with considerable conviction, that if he had simply waited for the hazmat team, none of this would have happened - that his decision to enter early was a failure of judgment that he should have known better than to make at his age, with his experience. He returned to the sequence of that evening repeatedly, reconstructing it, testing alternative decisions, unable to arrive at a version in which he was not culpable. This mental activity occupied long stretches of his evenings and early mornings.

To prevent those stretches from becoming too long or too quiet, Harjit began filling every available hour with company. He arranged family dinners on nights when none had been planned, lingered at the station longer than his shifts required, and became, in his wife's words, unusually reluctant to be alone in any room of the house. What he understood himself to be doing was keeping the thoughts at bay; what accumulated over months was a kind of exhaustion in the people around him, a subtle but growing friction with his wife, who felt simultaneously sought out and shut out - present in body but not in the conversation she actually wanted to have with him.

At work, the difficulties became harder to conceal. Harjit began requesting reassignment away from hospital handovers, citing administrative reasons. He delayed or avoided mandatory physical examinations, rescheduling twice before his supervisor noted the pattern. The ambulance itself - the smell of it, the equipment, the interior lighting that reminded him in some peripheral way of industrial spaces - had become a place he entered with effortful deliberation rather than professional ease.

What finally brought him to seek help was a near-miss: a moment at a handover bay when a nurse opened an alcohol swab beside him and Harjit, a man who had worked trauma scenes without flinching for twenty-eight years, had to excuse himself and stand outside in the cold for several minutes before he could return. He told his wife that evening. He is most afraid that the version of himself that walked confidently into emergencies is gone. He is hoping, cautiously, to be told that it is not.
